messages.subject: Re: Unmarked Covariate modeling
messages.body_plain:
Hi Imran,

Cluster size is an important issue that has not been addressed yet in
unmarked. Cluster size is not a transect-specific covariate, so it
might be difficult to formally include in this model. However, I think
you could model the abundance of clusters and then multiply your
*cluster abundance* estimate by the average number of individuals per
cluster to get a post-hoc estimate of population size. Let me think
more about this.

Could you be more specific about what you mean by effort? If you used
line-transects, you can specify the length of each transect in your
call to unmarkedFrameDS, which will account for that type of variation
in effort. Other types of variation in effort could be modeled as
covariates or included as a priori known effects using the offset()
function in your formula.

I'm not quite sure what you mean in your third question. If you have
multiple covariates, you can use a model selection process to find the
best model. If they are highly correlated, you could use PCA and then
include the PCs as covariates.

It is not currently possible to do multispecies model.

Here is some code that might help (I don't have your data so I can't
test this):

# Bin the data to create a response matrix
cuts <- seq(0, 100, by=10) # or something like c(10, 30, 60, 100)
y <- formatDistData(fha, "Dist", "TR", cuts) # Note that I used "TR"
and not "Clusters"

# Make sure the rows for the response are in the same order as your
covariate data
y <- y[rownames(covs1),]

# Create unmarkedFrame, assuming you have line-transect data recorded
in meters and
# transect lengths are the same.
umf <- unmarkedFrameDS(y=y, siteCovs=as.data.frame(covs1),
survey="line", unitsIn="m")

# Fit a model
m1 <- distsamp(~1 ~habitat, umf, keyfun="halfnorm", output="abund")

If you need more help, please try to use the functions and let us know
what error messages you get. Also, more details on your design are
necessary. Line or point transects? Were there any transects where you
did not observe any animals? etc...

Richard

http://groups.google.com/group/unmarked

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Unmarked Covariate modeling
messages.body_plain:
An important distinction in modeling cluster size is whether you observe cluster size without error or not.  If you do observe cluster size without error then it can be used, essentially, as a covariate on detection probability.  For example, see the attached paper -- I'm sure a variation of this could be applied to the unmarked distance sampling functionality. But Richard is super busy now so it would have to wait until September.
regards,
andy

messages.subject: student research assistant position (R programming/modeling/analysis)
messages.body_plain:
hi all,
 see information below regarding a student assistant position.  Very
compressed timeline, sorry for that.
regards
andy

Ecological Research Assistant Needed
Quantitative Ecology – Mathematical/Statistical Modeling, R
programming, Data Analysis

USGS PATUXENT WILDLIFE RESEARCH CENTER

The Quantitative Ecology Group at USGS Patuxent Wildlife Research
Center is searching for an extremely motivated and talented research
assistant to work at least 20 hours per week for approx 6-9 months
beginning as early as Aug. 2010.

The position involves data analysis, estimation, and modeling in
support of various projects focused on population, metapopulation,
community ecology, spatial sampling of animal populations, spatial
ecology, and wildlife surveys. The incumbent will design and develop
statistical software in the R programming environment. Knowledge of
the R programming environment is required. Must be highly motivated
and able to work independently. Other desired skills include knowledge
of likelihood and Bayesian methods of statistical inference, Markov
chain Monte Carlo, especially implementation in WinBUGS, and GIS.

The position requires completion of a B.S. or M.S. degree in any
related field. The ideal candidate has a graduate degree in Ecology,
Natural Resources or Statistics, and interested in the application of
quantitative methods to ecological problems as an element of his or
her graduate research.

Students are responsible for all costs of transportation to and from
Patuxent Wildlife Research Center. Salary depends on qualifications.

Principal Duty Station:
USGS Patuxent Wildlife Research Center
12100 Beech Forest Road
Laurel, Maryland 20708-4038

To apply, send the following to Andy Royle at the above address or via
email (aro...@usgs.gov) or FAX (301.497.5545) NO LATER THAN JUNE 29:

1) Letter of interest, professional interests, and career goals (if
any).
2) Piece of R code that does something interesting, useful,
efficiently, or in a novel way. (also describe what it does, just in
case).
3)  Resume, including relevant experience, list of relevant classes,
contact information and two or three reference contacts

messages.subject: manually fixing parameters?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ian and Richard,

I saw on http://github.com/ianfiske/unmarked/issues that you might be
adding the ability to manually fix parameters in unmarked models.  Was
this implemented in version 0.8-6?  This could be very useful, for
example, in an iterative approach to modeling in occ or colext if the
user wants to use model-averaged (observation-level) detection
parameters before constructing site-level occupancy models.

Best,

Giancarlo
